content: The apex beat, also referred to as the point of maximum impulse (PMI), is the furthest point laterally and inferiorly from the sternum where the cardiac impulse can be palpated. This impulse is generated by the heart's rotation, forward movement, and contact with the chest wall during systole. Under normal circumstances, the apex beat is palpable in the left fifth intercostal space, at the intersection with the left midclavicular line. In pediatric patients, the apex beat is typically located in the fourth intercostal space, medial to the nipple. In certain pathological conditions, the apex beat may be found in abnormal locations. For instance, in cases of dextrocardia, the apex beat may be palpated on the right side of the chest. A lateral and/or inferior displacement of the apex beat is often indicative of cardiac enlargement, a condition known as cardiomegaly. Additionally, the apex beat may be displaced by other factors, including pleural or pulmonary diseases, as well as structural deformities of the chest wall or thoracic vertebrae. There are instances where the apex beat may not be palpable. This can occur in individuals with a thick chest wall or in clinical scenarios where the stroke volume is significantly reduced, such as during ventricular tachycardia or states of shock. The characteristics of the apex beat can also provide critical diagnostic information. Conversely, an uncoordinated or dyskinetic apex beat, which involves a larger area than normal, is indicative of ventricular dysfunction. This may occur in the presence of a ventricular aneurysm, often following a myocardial infarction.
